title: Oll Rinkrank
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 196. Text from Wikisource („Oll Rinkrank (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: “Oll Rinkrank,” KHM 196, is told from first word to last in Low German, and the glossary carries the High German equivalent of every dialect form. A king promises his daughter to whoever can run over a glass mountain without falling; she goes along to steady her suitor, slips herself, and the mountain opens under her and closes again, leaving her deep underground as maid to an old fellow with a long grey beard — for so many years that she has grown old before she sees daylight again. What frees her is a small hatch left open, a beard pushed through it and a band pulled tight; the three rhymed calls at the door are all his, and the king’s justice at the end is done in a single sentence.

sentences.t: Dar war mal ’n König wän, un de har ’n Dochter hat:
sentences.l: There had once been a king, and he had had a daughter:
sentences.i: There was once a king, and he had a daughter:
sentences.n: The whole tale is told in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the old speech of the north, and not in the High German of most of the collection — the glossary gives the High German word for every dialect form. Here: “Dar” = da (there), “un” = und, “de” = der, “har … hat” = hatte … gehabt. The doubled past “war … wän” (= war … gewesen) is the dialect’s ordinary way of setting a story long ago.

sentences.t: un de har ’n glasen Barg maken laten, un har segt de dar över lopen kun, an to vallen, de schull sin Dochter to ’n Fro hebben.
sentences.l: and he had had a glass mountain made, and had said [that] whoever could run over it, without falling, he should have his daughter for a wife.
sentences.i: and he had had a mountain of glass built, and had declared that whoever could run across it without falling should have his daughter to wife.
sentences.n: The trap in this line is “an”: it is not the preposition here but Low German for ohne — “an to vallen” = ohne zu fallen, without falling. The same word returns as “an dat he valt” below. “glasen Barg” = gläserner Berg; “maken laten” = machen lassen. “de … de” doubles the relative — the first is ‘whoever’, the second picks it up again as ‘he’, a habit of the dialect. The square brackets in the literal supply a ‘that’ the German does not print.

sentences.t: Do is dar ok en, de mag de Königsdochter so gärn liden, de vragt den König of he sin Dochter nich hebben schal?
sentences.l: Then there is also one, who likes the king’s-daughter so gladly, he asks the king whether he is not to have his daughter?
sentences.i: Now there was one who was so fond of the king’s daughter that he asked the king whether he might not have her.
sentences.n: From here the tale tells itself in the present tense — “is”, “vragt”, “segt” — where English wants a past; the literal keeps the present so the shape stays visible. “gärn liden mögen” (gern leiden mögen) is the ordinary way of saying one is fond of somebody. “of” = ob (whether); “vragt” = fragt. The question mark after what is really an indirect question is the 1857 printing’s own.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ segt de König, „wenn he dar över den Barg lopen kan, an dat he valt, den schal he är hebben.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” says the king, “if he can run over the mountain there, without that he falls, then shall he have her.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the king, “if he can run across the mountain without falling, then he shall have her.”
sentences.n: “an dat” = ohne daß, and it is the same “an” as in the line above. “den” here is not the article but Low German for dann (then) — it will keep coming back in that sense. “är” = ihr/sie (her).

sentences.t: Do segt de Königsdochter den wil se dar mit hüm över lopen un wil hüm hollen, wen he war vallen schul.
sentences.l: Then says the king’s-daughter [that] then she will run over it with him and will hold him, if he should fall somewhere.
sentences.i: Then the king’s daughter said that in that case she would run across with him and hold him if he should chance to fall.
sentences.n: Reported speech with no “dat” (daß) to introduce it — the dialect simply runs the clause straight on, and the literal supplies the bracketed ‘that’. “wen” is wenn (if), not wen (whom); “war” here is wo (where, somewhere), not war (was). Both are constant traps in this tale. “hüm” = ihm/ihn.

sentences.t: Do lopt se dar mit ’nanner över, un as se dar miden up sünt, do glit de Königsdochter ut un valt, un de Glasbarg de deit sick apen, un se schütt darin hendal:
sentences.l: Then they run over it with one another, and as they are midway up on it, then the king’s-daughter slips and falls, and the glass-mountain it opens itself, and she shoots down into it:
sentences.i: So the two of them ran across together, and when they were halfway up, the king’s daughter slipped and fell, and the glass mountain opened, and she shot down inside it:
sentences.n: “sünt” is sind (are) here — not the Sankt of a saint’s name that the same spelling carries elsewhere in the collection. “mit ’nanner” = miteinander; “miden up” = mitten darauf; “ut glien” = ausgleiten, to slip; “apen don” = aufmachen, to open. “schütt … hendal” = schießt hinab.

sentences.t: un de Brögam de kan nich sen war se herdör kamen is, den de Barg het sick glick wär to dan.
sentences.l: and the bridegroom he cannot see where she has got through, for the mountain has at once shut itself to again.
sentences.i: and the bridegroom could not see where she had gone through, for the mountain had closed itself up again at once.
sentences.n: “den” here is a third sense again: denn (for, because), alongside the dann and the article the same spelling carries. “wär” = wieder (again), not wäre; “to dan” = zugetan, shut to, with the separable zu- of zutun. “Brögam” = Bräutigam.

sentences.t: Do jammert un went he so väl, un de König is ok so trorig un let den Barg dar wedder weg bräken
sentences.l: Then he wails and weeps so much, and the king is also so sorrowful and has the mountain there broken away again
sentences.i: Then he lamented and wept so bitterly, and the king too was so sorrowful that he had the mountain broken away again
sentences.n: “went” = weint (weeps); “väl” = viel; “trorig” = traurig. “weg bräken” = wegbrechen, and its particle stands apart from the verb exactly as a separable prefix does in High German.

sentences.t: un ment he wil är wedder ut krigen, man se könt de Stä ni finnen wär se hendal vallen is.
sentences.l: and thinks he will get her out again, but they cannot find the place where she has fallen down.
sentences.i: thinking he would get her out again; but they could not find the spot where she had fallen through.
sentences.n: Two words to watch here. “ment” is meint (thinks, intends) — not the ‘nur’ the spelling means elsewhere in the collection. And “man” is Low German for aber (but), not the pronoun man. “Stä” = Stätte/Stelle; “ni” = nicht; “wär” is wo (where) this time, not wieder.

sentences.t: Ünnertüsken is de Königsdochter ganz dep in de Grunt in ’n grote Höl kamen.
sentences.l: In the meantime the king’s-daughter has come quite deep in the ground into a great cave.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the king’s daughter had come deep down in the earth into a great cavern.
sentences.n: “Ünnertüsken” = unterdessen (meanwhile); “dep” = tief; “Grunt” = Grund, the ground or the depths; “Höl” = Höhle. The dialect keeps the older consonants that High German shifted: dep for tief, to for zu, ik for ich, maken for machen.

sentences.t: Do kumt är dar ’n ollen Kärl mit ’n ganzen langen grauen Bart to möt,
sentences.l: Then there comes to meet her an old fellow with a quite long grey beard,
sentences.i: Then an old fellow with a very long grey beard came to meet her,
sentences.n: “to möt kamen” = entgegenkommen, to come to meet somebody — “möt” belongs to that phrase and is not the verb müssen here. “Kärl” = Kerl; “oll” = alt, and it is the word that gives the tale its title, Oll Rinkrank, Old Rinkrank.

sentences.t: un de segt wen se sin Magd wäsen wil un all don wat he bevelt, den schal se läven bliven, anners wil he är ümbringen.
sentences.l: and he says if she will be his maid and do all that he commands, then shall she stay alive, otherwise he will kill her.
sentences.i: and he said that if she would be his servant and do everything he ordered, she should stay alive; otherwise he would kill her.
sentences.n: “wäsen” = sein (to be); “don” = tun (to do), not the noun Ton; “bevelt” = befiehlt; “läven bliven” = am Leben bleiben; “ümbringen” = umbringen, to kill. The threat is stated flatly, and the tale spends no word on it.

sentences.t: Do deit se all wat he är segt.
sentences.l: Then she does all that he tells her.
sentences.i: So she did everything he told her.
sentences.n: “deit” = tut, the dialect’s short form of don/tun; “är” = ihr (to her).

sentences.t: ’S Morgens den kricht he sin Ledder ut de Task un legt de an den Barg un sticht darmit to ’n Barg henut: un den lukt he de Ledder na sick ümhoch mit sick henup.
sentences.l: Of a morning then he gets his ladder out of his pocket and lays it against the mountain and climbs with it out to the top of the mountain: and then he draws the ladder up after himself, up with him.
sentences.i: Of a morning he would take his ladder out of his pocket and set it against the mountain and climb out by it; and then he drew the ladder up after him.
sentences.n: “’S Morgens” = des Morgens, the old genitive of time, ‘of a morning.’ The word to watch is “sticht”: it is steigt (climbs), from Low German stigen, and not sticht (stabs), which the same spelling means in High German. “Ledder” = Leiter; “Task” = Tasche; “lukt” = zieht, pulls; and “henut”, “ümhoch”, “henup” pile the directions up the way the dialect likes.

sentences.t: Un den mut se sin Äten kaken und sin Bedd maken un all sin Arbeit don,
sentences.l: And then she must cook his food and make his bed and do all his work,
sentences.i: And then she had to cook his food and make his bed and do all his work,
sentences.n: “Äten” = Essen; “kaken” = kochen; “don” = tun. The single “und” spelled out in full here, among all the dialect “un”, is the 1857 printing’s own inconsistency and is left as it stands.

sentences.t: un den, wen he wedder in Hus kumt, den bringt he alltit ’n Hüpen Golt un Sülver mit.
sentences.l: and then, when he comes into the house again, then he always brings a heap of gold and silver with him.
sentences.i: and whenever he came home again, he always brought a heap of gold and silver with him.
sentences.n: “alltit” = allezeit, always; “Hüpen” = Haufen; “Golt”, “Sülver” = Gold, Silber. “bringt … mit” is separable mitbringen, its particle waiting at the end.

sentences.t: As se al väl jaren bi em wäsen is un al ganz olt wurden is,
sentences.l: When she has already been many years with him and has already become quite old,
sentences.i: When she had been many years with him and had grown quite old,
sentences.n: “al” = schon (already); “väl jaren” = viele Jahre; “bi em” = bei ihm. “wurden” here is geworden, the past participle, not the plural preterite the spelling means in High German.

sentences.t: do het he är Fro Mansrot, un se möt hüm oll Rinkrank heten.
sentences.l: then he calls her Mistress Mansrot, and she must call him Old Rinkrank.
sentences.i: then he called her Mistress Mansrot, and she had to call him Old Rinkrank.
sentences.n: “heten” = heißen, here in its older transitive sense, ‘to call somebody something’, rather than ‘to be called’. What Mansrot means, and why she is made to answer to it, is not settled; the text simply gives the two names and moves on. Rinkrank has been read as something like ‘crooked ring’, but that too is a guess.

sentences.t: Do is he ok ins enmal ut, do makt se hüm sin Bedd un waskt sin Schöttels, un do makt se de Dören un Vensters all dicht to,
sentences.l: Then he is also once out, then she makes his bed for him and washes his dishes, and then she shuts the doors and windows all tight,
sentences.i: Then one day he was out; and she made his bed and washed his dishes, and then she shut all the doors and windows fast,
sentences.n: “ok” is auch (also, too), not the ‘again’ that would be wedder. “ins enmal” doubles the word for ‘once’ — “ins” is einmal here, not in das. “Schöttels” = Schüsseln (dishes); “Vensters” = Fenster; “dicht to maken” = dicht zumachen, to shut tight.

sentences.t: un do is dar so ’n Schuf wäsen, war ’t Lecht herin schint het, dat let se apen.
sentences.l: and there had been such a sliding shutter there, where the light had shone in, that she leaves open.
sentences.i: but there was a sliding shutter there through which the light used to shine, and that one she left open.
sentences.n: “Schuf” is a sliding hatch or shutter (High German Schub, Schieber) — the same opening the tale calls “Luk” (Luke, a hatch) further on. “’t” here is dat = das, the article, not the pronoun ‘it’; “Lecht” = Licht; “schint” = scheint. Putting “dat” first — ‘that one she leaves open’ — throws the weight onto the thing itself, as German freely does.

sentences.t: As d’ oll Rinkrank do wedder kumt, do klopt he an sin Dör un röpt „Fro Mansrot, do mi d’ Dör apen.“
sentences.l: When old Rinkrank then comes again, then he knocks at his door and calls “Mistress Mansrot, open the door for me.”
sentences.i: When Old Rinkrank came back, he knocked at his door and called, “Mistress Mansrot, open the door for me.”
sentences.n: “d’” is the article de (der/die/das) worn down to a single letter — “d’ oll Rinkrank”, “d’ Dör”. It is not the elided verb ending the same mark carries elsewhere. “do … apen” = tu … auf; “Dör” = Tür; “klopt” = klopft; “röpt” = ruft.

sentences.t: „Na,“ segt se, „ik do di, oll Rinkrank, d’ Dör nich apen.“
sentences.l: “No,” says she, “I do not open the door for you, old Rinkrank.”
sentences.i: “No,” said she, “I will not open the door for you, Old Rinkrank.”
sentences.n: “Na” is the flat refusal nein, and not the High German particle na. “ik” = ich; “di” = dir. The negative “nich” comes late, just before the particle “apen”, exactly where High German would put it.

sentences.t: Do segt he
sentences.l: Then he says
sentences.n: The printing runs the speech straight into the song that follows, with no colon.

sentences.t:
„hir sta ik arme Rinkrank
up min söventein Benen lank
up min en vergüllen Vot,
Fro Mansrot, wask mi d’ Schöttels.“
sentences.l:
“here stand I poor Rinkrank
on my seventeen legs long
on my one gilded foot,
Mistress Mansrot, wash me the dishes.”
sentences.i:
“Here I stand, poor Rinkrank,
on my seventeen long legs,
on my one gilded foot —
Mistress Mansrot, wash my dishes.”
sentences.n: The chant comes three times, and only its last line changes: dishes, then bed, then door. “hir” = hier; “sta” = stehe, a statement and not the imperative the same form can be; “up” = auf; “min” = mein; “Vot” = Fuß; “vergüllen” = vergoldet. “söventein Benen lank” is genuinely arguable: it can be read as ‘seventeen long legs’ or as ‘seventeen legs long’, that is, as a measure of his height — the tale never says which, and this rendering keeps the first. In the German, Rinkrank and lank chime, and Vot answers Mansrot; Lectorium’s English does not rhyme.

sentences.t: „’k heb din Schöttels al wusken“ segt se.
sentences.l: “I have washed your dishes already,” says she.
sentences.i: “I have already washed your dishes,” said she.
sentences.n: “’k” is ik (ich) worn down to a single consonant leaning on its verb; “heb” = habe, not the imperative of heben; “wusken” = gewaschen — Low German regularly drops the ge- of the past participle. “al” = schon.

sentences.t: Do segt he wedder
sentences.l: Then he says again
sentences.n: “wedder” = wieder.

sentences.t:
„hir sta ik arme Rinkrank
up min söventein Benen lank,
up min en vergüllen Vot,
Fro Mansrot, mak mi ’t Bedd.“
sentences.l:
“here stand I poor Rinkrank
on my seventeen legs long,
on my one gilded foot,
Mistress Mansrot, make me the bed.”
sentences.i:
“Here I stand, poor Rinkrank,
on my seventeen long legs,
on my one gilded foot —
Mistress Mansrot, make my bed.”
sentences.n: The same chant, word for word, with only the last line changed; the English keeps the same wording so the reader can see that the German did not move. “mak” = mach; “’t Bedd” = dat Bedd, das Bett.

sentences.t: „’k heb din Bedd al makt“ segt se.
sentences.l: “I have made your bed already,” says she.
sentences.i: “I have already made your bed,” said she.
sentences.n: “makt” here is gemacht, another past participle without its ge-. The same spelling is also the plain present ‘makes’ elsewhere in the tale.

sentences.t: Do segt he wedder
sentences.l: Then he says again
sentences.n: The third and last time, and this time what he demands is the door itself.

sentences.t:
„hir sta ik arme Rinkrank
up min söventein Benen lank,
up min en vergüllen Vot,
Fro Mansrot, do mi d’ Dör apen.“
sentences.l:
“here stand I poor Rinkrank
on my seventeen legs long,
on my one gilded foot,
Mistress Mansrot, open the door for me.”
sentences.i:
“Here I stand, poor Rinkrank,
on my seventeen long legs,
on my one gilded foot —
Mistress Mansrot, open the door for me.”
sentences.n: The last of the three, and the line she has already refused him is now the whole point of the song. “do … apen” = tu … auf, open up.

sentences.t: Do löpt he all runt üm sin Hus to un süt dat de lütke Luk dar apen is, do denkt he
sentences.l: Then he runs all round about his house and sees that the little hatch there is open, then he thinks
sentences.i: Then he ran right round his house and saw that the little hatch stood open, and thought
sentences.n: “löpt” = läuft; “runt üm … to” = rundherum; “lütke” = klein, a word the north uses constantly; “Luk” = Luke, the hatch — the same opening called “Schuf” above; “süt” = sieht. “denkt” is he thinks, third person, and not the plural imperative the spelling is elsewhere.

sentences.t: „du schast doch ins tosen wat se dar wol makt, warüm dat se mi d’ Dör wol nich apen don wil.“
sentences.l: “you shall just once take a look at what she is doing there, why she will not open the door for me.”
sentences.i: “I had better take a look at what she is up to in there, and why she will not open the door for me.”
sentences.n: He talks to himself in the second person — “du schast” = du sollst — where English says ‘I had better’. “ins” is again einmal, ‘just once’; “tosen” = zusehen; “warüm dat” = warum daß, a doubled conjunction the dialect likes; “wol” = wohl, the particle of supposition.

sentences.t: Do wil he dar dör kiken un kan den Kop dar ni dör krigen van sin langen Bart.
sentences.l: Then he wants to look through there and cannot get his head through it because of his long beard.
sentences.i: Then he wanted to look through, and could not get his head through for his long beard.
sentences.n: “kiken” = gucken, to look; “dör” = durch; “Kop” = Kopf; “van” = von, here in its causal sense, ‘for, because of’.

sentences.t: Do stekt he sin Bart dar erst dör de Luk, un as he de dar hendör het,
sentences.l: Then he puts his beard first through the hatch, and when he has it through there,
sentences.i: So he pushed his beard through the hatch first, and when he had it through,
sentences.n: “stekt” = steckt; “erst” = zuerst; “hendör” = hindurch. The beard going first is the detail the whole trap turns on.

sentences.t: do geit Fro Mansrot bi un schuft de Luk grad to mit ’n Bant, de se dar an bunnen het,
sentences.l: then Mistress Mansrot goes to it and shoves the hatch straight shut with a cord that she has tied on to it,
sentences.i: then Mistress Mansrot stepped up and shoved the hatch shut with a cord she had tied to it,
sentences.n: “bi gan” = beigehen, to set to, to get to work at something. “grad” = gerade (straight, at once) — plain Low German here, and not the Alemannic word the same spelling is in the Swiss tales. “schuft” = schiebt, from the same root as the Schuf itself; “Bant” = Band, a cord; “bunnen” = gebunden.

sentences.t: un de Bart blift darin vast sitten.
sentences.l: and the beard stays sitting fast in it.
sentences.i: and the beard was held fast in it.
sentences.n: “blift” = bleibt; “vast sitten” = festsitzen, to be stuck fast.

sentences.t: Do fangt he so jammerlik an to kriten, dat deit üm so sär:
sentences.l: Then he begins to shriek so piteously, it hurts him so sore:
sentences.i: Then he began to shriek so piteously, for it hurt him so badly:
sentences.n: “fangt … an” is anfangen, third person here and not the imperative it is elsewhere; “kriten” = schreien, to shriek or wail; “jammerlik” = jämmerlich. “dat deit üm sär” = das tut ihm weh; “sär” is the same old word as English ‘sore’.

sentences.t: un do bidd’t he är se mag üm wedder los laten.
sentences.l: and then he begs her [that] she may let him loose again.
sentences.i: and then he begged her to let him loose again.
sentences.n: Again reported speech with no daß, and again the literal supplies the bracketed ‘that’. “bidd’t” = bittet; “mag” here is the ‘may’ of a request rather than ‘likes’; “los laten” = loslassen.

sentences.t: Do segt se er nich as bet he är de Ledder deit, war he mit to ’n Barg herut sticht.
sentences.l: Then says she not sooner than until he gives her the ladder that he climbs out of the mountain with.
sentences.i: But she said, not before he gave her the ladder he climbed out of the mountain with.
sentences.n: “er” here is eher (sooner, before) and not er (he) — the most easily mistaken little word in the tale. “as bet” = als bis; “deit” = tut, here in the sense ‘hands over’; “war … mit” is womit, split apart the way German splits its da- and wo- compounds; “sticht” is once more steigt, climbs.

sentences.t: Do mag he willen oder nich, he mot är seggen war de Ledder is.
sentences.l: Then he may want to or not, he must tell her where the ladder is.
sentences.i: Whether he would or not, he had to tell her where the ladder was.
sentences.n: “willen” is the verb wollen (to want), not the noun Wille; “mot” = muß; “war” is again wo (where).

sentences.t: Do bint se ’n ganzen langen Bant dar an de Schuf, un do legt se de Ledder an un sticht to ’n Barg herut:
sentences.l: Then she ties a quite long cord there on to the shutter, and then she sets the ladder up and climbs out of the mountain:
sentences.i: Then she tied a very long cord to the shutter, set the ladder up and climbed out of the mountain:
sentences.n: The cord is what keeps the hatch shut on his beard while she goes; she leaves him fast. “bint” = bindet; “legt … an” = legt an, sets up against; “to ’n Barg herut” = zum Berg heraus.

sentences.t: un as se baven is, do lukt se de Schuf apen.
sentences.l: and when she is above, then she pulls the shutter open.
sentences.i: and when she was up above, she pulled the shutter open.
sentences.n: “baven” = oben, the same old word as English ‘above’. She opens it only once she is safely out — the tale does not say what becomes of him in the meantime.

sentences.t: Do geit se na är Vader hen un vertelt wo dat är all gan is.
sentences.l: Then she goes to her father and tells how it has all gone for her.
sentences.i: Then she went to her father and told him all that had befallen her.
sentences.n: “wo” here is wie (how), not wo (where); the two swap places in this dialect. “vertelt” = erzählt; “gan” = gegangen; “na … hen” = hin zu, off to.

sentences.t: Do freut de König sick so un är Brögam is dar ok noch,
sentences.l: Then the king rejoices so, and her bridegroom is still there too,
sentences.i: Then the king rejoiced greatly, and her bridegroom was still there too,
sentences.n: The tale gives no hint of how the years have passed for him while she grew “ganz olt” underground; the printing simply does not make the connection. “sick freuen” = sich freuen.

sentences.t: un do gat se hen un gravt den Barg up un finnt den ollen Rinkrank mit all sin Golt ün Sülver darin.
sentences.l: and then they go and dig the mountain up and find old Rinkrank inside with all his gold and silver.
sentences.i: and then they went and dug the mountain open and found Old Rinkrank inside with all his gold and silver.
sentences.n: “gat” = gehen, they go; “up graven” = aufgraben, to dig open. The “ün” before Sülver is the printing’s own variant of “un” (und) — not the “ün” meaning ihm that the spelling carries elsewhere.

sentences.t: Do let de König den ollen Rinkrank dot maken, un all sin Sülver un Golt nimt he mit.
sentences.l: Then the king has old Rinkrank put to death, and all his silver and gold he takes with him.
sentences.i: Then the king had Old Rinkrank put to death, and took all his silver and gold with him.
sentences.n: “dot maken” = totmachen, to kill — said flatly and in four words, with no more attention than the gold gets. “let … maken” = läßt machen, has it done.

sentences.t: Do kricht de Königsdochter den ollen Brögam noch ton Mann, un se lävt recht vergnögt un herrlich un in Freuden.
sentences.l: Then the king’s-daughter gets the old bridegroom for a husband after all, and she lives right merrily and splendidly and in joy.
sentences.i: So the king’s daughter got her old bridegroom for a husband after all, and lived contentedly, in splendour and joy.
sentences.n: “ton” is to ’n = zum (for a) — not the noun Ton. “kricht” = kriegt; “lävt” = lebt. “herrlich un in Freuden” is the collection’s stock closing formula, ‘in splendour and joy’.

glossary.an: Low German (Plattdeutsch): ohne — without (an to vallen = ohne zu fallen; an dat he valt = ohne daß er fällt); also the preposition an — at, on, against
glossary.barg: Low German (Plattdeutsch): der Berg — mountain (de Glasbarg, the glass mountain)
glossary.d: Low German (Plattdeutsch): d’ = de — the (der/die/das, the article worn down to a single letter: d’ Dör = die Tür)
glossary.den: Low German (Plattdeutsch): dann; denn — then; for, because; also the article den (acc. masc.)
glossary.denkt: Low German (Plattdeutsch): denkt — thinks (denken, 3rd sg. present)
glossary.di: Low German (Plattdeutsch): dir, dich — you, to you
glossary.do: Low German (Plattdeutsch): da, dann — then, there; also tun — to do (do mi d’ Dör apen = tu mir die Tür auf; ik do di … nich apen = ich tue dir … nicht auf)
glossary.don: Low German (Plattdeutsch): tun — to do (apen don = aufmachen, to open)
glossary.dör: Low German (Plattdeutsch): die Tür — door (d’ Dör = die Tür); also durch — through (dar dör kiken = da durch gucken)
glossary.er: Low German (Plattdeutsch): eher — sooner, before (‘se segt er nich as bet …’ = sie sagt nicht eher, als bis …); also er, he
glossary.fangt: Low German (Plattdeutsch): fängt — begins (anfangen, separable: fangt … an; 3rd sg. present)
glossary.gan: Low German (Plattdeutsch): gehen; gegangen — to go; gone (past participle without the ge-: wo dat är all gan is)
glossary.grad: Low German (Plattdeutsch): gerade — straight, at once (grad to schuven = gerade zuschieben)
glossary.gärn: Low German (Plattdeutsch): gern — gladly, willingly (gärn liden mögen = gern leiden mögen, to be fond of)
glossary.har: Low German (Plattdeutsch): hatte — had (hebben = haben, 3rd sg. past; har … hat = hatte … gehabt)
glossary.hat: Low German (Plattdeutsch): gehabt — had (past participle of hebben = haben, without the ge-)
glossary.heb: Low German (Plattdeutsch): habe — have (hebben = haben, 1st sg. present; ’k heb = ich habe)
glossary.het: Low German (Plattdeutsch): hat — has (hebben = haben, 3rd sg. present); also heißt — calls (heten = heißen, 3rd sg. present: do het he är Fro Mansrot = da heißt er sie Frau Mansrot)
glossary.ins: Low German (Plattdeutsch): einmal — once, just once (ins enmal = einmal; du schast doch ins tosen = sieh doch einmal zu)
glossary.ja: ja — yes (the plain affirmation); also, as a particle, surely, after all
glossary.kamen: Low German (Plattdeutsch): kommen; gekommen — to come; come (past participle, without the ge-)
glossary.lank: Low German (Plattdeutsch): lang — long (up min söventein Benen lank: whether this means ‘seventeen long legs’ or ‘seventeen legs long’, a measure of height, is arguable)
glossary.mal: Low German (Plattdeutsch): einmal — once (dar war mal = da war einmal)
glossary.man: Low German (Plattdeutsch): aber, nur — but, only (‘man se könt de Stä ni finnen’ = aber sie können die Stelle nicht finden)
glossary.mann: der Mann — man; husband (ton Mann kriegen = zum Mann bekommen, to get for a husband)
glossary.ment: Low German (Plattdeutsch): meint — thinks, intends (menen = meinen, 3rd sg. present)
glossary.möt: Low German (Plattdeutsch): muß — must (möten = müssen, 3rd sg. present); also in to möt kamen = entgegenkommen, to come to meet somebody
glossary.n: Low German (Plattdeutsch): ’n = en — a, an (ein/einen: ’n König = ein König; mit ’nanner = miteinander)
glossary.na: Low German (Plattdeutsch): nach, zu — to, toward (na är Vader hen = zu ihrem Vater hin; na sick = nach sich); also nee, nein — no, the flat refusal (‘Na,’ segt se)
glossary.s: Low German (Plattdeutsch): ’S = des — of the (’S Morgens = des Morgens, of a morning)
glossary.schint: Low German (Plattdeutsch): geschienen — shone (schinen = scheinen; past participle without the ge-, with het = hat)
glossary.sta: Low German (Plattdeutsch): stehe — stand (stan = stehen, 1st sg. present: hir sta ik = hier stehe ich)
glossary.sticht: Low German (Plattdeutsch): steigt — climbs (stigen = steigen, 3rd sg. present) — not sticht, stabs
glossary.sünt: Low German (Plattdeutsch): sind — are (sein, 3rd pl. present)
glossary.t: Low German (Plattdeutsch): ’t = dat — the (das, the article reduced: ’t Bedd = das Bett, ’t Lecht = das Licht)
glossary.ton: Low German (Plattdeutsch): ton = to ’n = zum — to the, for a (ton Mann = zum Mann)
glossary.war: Low German (Plattdeutsch): wo — where (war se hendal vallen is = wo sie hinabgefallen ist); also war, was
glossary.willen: Low German (Plattdeutsch): wollen — to want (he mag willen oder nich = er mag wollen oder nicht)
glossary.wo: Low German (Plattdeutsch): wie — how (wo dat är all gan is = wie es ihr alles ergangen ist); also wo, where
glossary.wurden: Low German (Plattdeutsch): geworden — become (past participle of werden)
glossary.wär: Low German (Plattdeutsch): wieder; wo — again; where (het sick wär to dan = hat sich wieder zugetan; wär se vallen is = wo sie gefallen ist)
glossary.üm: Low German (Plattdeutsch): ihm, ihn — him, to him (dat deit üm so sär = das tut ihm weh); also um — around (runt üm sin Hus = rund um sein Haus)
glossary.ün: Low German (Plattdeutsch): und — and (the printing’s variant of un in ‘Golt ün Sülver’)
